sections.title: Identification
sections.text: Suillus luteus, the slippery jack, is a bolete with a cap that starts convex and flattens with age, usually chestnut to yellowish brown. Its cuticle becomes thickly slimy and glossy in wet weather and separates readily from the flesh; it looks more matte when dry. The cap is most often about 5–12 cm across, with variation among sources and specimens.

sections.title: Pores, stem and flesh
sections.text: The fertile surface consists of short to moderately long tubes ending in small, round to slightly angular pores. They are pale yellow at first, becoming yellow to olive-yellow with age. A white partial veil may cover the pores on young specimens. The whitish to pale-yellow stem normally bears a broad, membranous ring; its lower surface often develops violet to brown tones with age. Brownish glandular dots are common above the ring. The white to pale-yellow flesh generally does not blue when cut; the spore print is cinnamon brown to ochre.

sections.title: Habitat and similar species
sections.text: This ectomycorrhizal species grows on the ground with pines (Pinus), often in groups, mainly from late summer into autumn. It is widespread in its Eurasian range and has been introduced to several other regions. The ring often distinguishes S. luteus from Suillus granulatus, which lacks one, but the ring may disappear on old specimens; consider the full set of features and the associated tree.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: Suillus luteus is listed as edible by the DGfM and VAPKO; the US Forest Service field guide advises removing the cap skin. Culinary recommendations do not establish a specimen’s identity: never eat a wild mushroom based on an image alone.

traits: Cap usually 5–12 cm across, convex then flattening, chestnut to yellowish brown, very slimy and glossy when wet; cuticle readily separable
Small round to slightly angular pores, yellow then olive-yellow with age; tubes, never gills
Whitish to pale-yellow stem, normally with a broad membranous ring whose underside often becomes violet to brown
Brownish glandular dots common on the stem above the ring
White to pale-yellow flesh, generally unchanged when cut; cinnamon-brown to ochre spore print
On the ground with pines (Pinus), often in groups, mainly from late summer into autumn
safetyNote: The DGfM and VAPKO list Suillus luteus as edible, and the US Forest Service field guide recommends removing the cap skin. Food recommendations cannot identify a specimen: never eat a wild mushroom based on a photo alone. If symptoms occur after ingestion, contact poison control or emergency services promptly.
